summary: Location services need a device to find its Location Information Server, which is hard behind a residential gateway. This document defines discovery using IP addresses and reverse DNS.

eli5.summary: Your home router hides your device from the outside. This helps the device find the place that knows where it is, using the address book.

questions: find location information server behind a gateway
how does a device find its location information server
what is reverse dns lis discovery
why does a residential gateway break lis discovery
subtitle: How a device behind a home router can find its Location Information Server by turning its IP address into reverse DNS names.

tldr.problem: A device needs to find the Location Information Server (LIS) of its access network, but DHCP-based discovery usually fails when a residential gateway sits in between.
tldr.mechanism: The device collects its IP addresses, turns each into a reverse DNS name in in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa, and runs the LIS discovery lookup on that name and on shorter versions of it.
tldr.outcome: It is a transitional (UNSAF) fallback that is tried only after DHCP discovery fails, until gateways that follow RFC 5986 are widely deployed.

today: RFC 7216 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text calls it a transitional solution, to be made obsolete when gateways that follow RFC 5986 are widely deployed.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Location Information Server (LIS) is a service in an access network that uses knowledge of the network topology to generate location information for Devices. A Device must be configured with the right LIS, and RFC 5986 describes doing this with DHCP (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) as input to U-NAPTR discovery.

Residential gateways, or home routers, mostly get in the way. A new DHCP option takes a long time to deploy everywhere, and the millions of gateways already in homes and businesses are not expected, and are likely not able, to provide the functions that RFC 5986 describes. This RFC therefore defines a way for a Device to build a domain name for discovery from its own IP addresses, with no help from the gateway.

In some cases the method is a UNilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF, RFC 3424) method, so it is considered transitional.
sections.eli5: Some places can tell a computer where it is, but the computer has to find them first. The usual way of finding them is blocked by the home router.

sections.title: The Residential Gateway Problem
sections.content:
In the typical topology there is an access network run by an ISP, which contains the LIS, and a residential network behind the gateway. Because the area served by a gateway is small, the ISP can provide location information that identifies the residence. The goal is to find the LIS in the access network.

A gateway can combine a modem, Ethernet switch, wireless access point, router, NAT, DHCP server, DNS relay and firewall. NAT has the greatest effect. Devices behind it get a generic configuration with no information about the ISP network, and their DNS setting usually points to a DNS relay on the gateway.

The firewall matters too: a port filter may block traffic on certain TCP and UDP ports, so a solution must allow for blocked traffic. Replacing or updating gateways is hard to justify, so the RFC describes a method that works without any assistance from the network.
sections.eli5: The router gives every device a note with no mention of the internet company. So the devices do not know who could tell them where they are.

sections.title: From IP Address to Domain Name
sections.content:
LIS discovery uses a DNS-based Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS) process whose input is a domain name. This RFC supplies alternative names derived from the Device's IP addresses, taken from the reverse DNS trees in-addr.arpa. and ip6.arpa.. After DHCP-based discovery has failed, a Device does the following:

  1. Collect the IP addresses that refer to it.
  2. Convert each into a name in the reverse tree.
  3. Run the DDDS process on those names.
  4. Shorten the names and repeat.

The addresses are ordered by proximity, with addresses used on adjacent segments favored over public or remote ones, and addresses on local interfaces come first. A Device can use STUN (RFC 5389) with a Binding Request and read the XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS in the response to learn its public, reflexive address. It MAY also use PCP, UPnP or NAT-PMP, which can report the gateway's external address, but these are not mandated.

The domain name for each address is the name that would be used for a reverse DNS lookup. IPv4 names follow Section 3.5 of RFC 1035 and IPv6 names follow Section 2.5 of RFC 3596.
sections.eli5: The computer looks at its own address and writes it backwards as an entry to look up. That entry points to who runs the location service.

sections.title: Shortened Names
sections.content:
If the search on the full name finds no NAPTR record with the desired service tag (for example LIS:HELD), the search is repeated on shorter names so that one DNS record can cover many addresses.

  • IPv4: the name SHOULD be shortened successively by one and two labels. This corresponds to a /24 or /16 prefix.
  • IPv6: the name SHOULD be shortened successively by 16, 18, 20 and 24 labels. This corresponds to a /64, /56, /48 or /32 prefix.

This gives operators flexibility without many more DNS names to search. It attaches no other significance to these zone cuts and creates no classful addressing hierarchy. If no LIS is found, no more than five U-NAPTR resolutions are invoked per IP address.
sections.eli5: If the exact house is not in the address book, the computer tries the street, then the neighborhood. One page for the whole street saves writing a page for every house.

sections.title: When to Use It and How to Deploy It
sections.content:
The DHCP method of RFC 5986 MUST be tried on all local interfaces first. This method is used when DHCP is unavailable, when the DHCP server gives no access network domain name, or when a request to the resulting LIS returns a HELD notLocatable error or equivalent.

Private addresses (for example from RFC 1918 ranges) can be used as input, but only if the DNS server used has a view of the same address space. Public DNS servers cannot give useful records for private addresses. The method assumes the public, reflexive address is controlled by the access network provider or a related party, so that provider can update the matching reverse DNS record. A VPN or other tunnel may stop the entity behind the public address from providing location.

Access network providers SHOULD publish NAPTR records for each public IP address used by Devices, and a DNS server inside a NAT SHOULD also include records for the private range. A network that does NAT SHOULD provide NAPTR records that reference a LIS endpoint with a public address. A record higher in the tree applies to all addresses below it, and a record lower down overrides it, so exceptions are possible.
sections.eli5: This trick is the backup plan. The computer tries the normal way first, and the internet company has to write the right entries in its address book for the backup to work.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Measures must be taken so that location information does not reach unauthorized parties. The mechanism here covers a device learning its own location, which the RFC assumes is not a privacy risk. The remaining risks are the use of geolocation by applications, covered by the framework in RFC 6280, and abuse of the location configuration protocol.

If a third party could spoof the location configuration protocol, this mechanism could help them find the right server to attack for a given IP address, so a LIS has to meet the security requirements of its protocol. Also, a Device that discovers a LIS this way MUST NOT give it additional information that might reveal its position, such as the measurements in RFC 7105, unless it has a secondary way to check the LIS is authentic, such as a white list.
sections.eli5: Do not tell a stranger extra clues about where you are until you are sure they are who they say they are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations in RFC 5986 apply, and the main concern is an attacker impersonating a LIS. The identity of a LIS is public information, so letting a third party discover it adds no concern.

The new concern is a falsified IP address. Even though STUN messages are protected by a MESSAGE-INTEGRITY attribute (an HMAC using a shared secret), an on-path attacker can alter source and destination addresses to give a Device a falsified address. The result could be denial of service or a deliberately misleading service. If the attacker controls the falsified address, misleading but verifiable DNS records could point to a malicious LIS that gives false location. No specific mechanism prevents this; the suggested remedy is independent verification, for example from a trusted source of location information.

Private address space effectively prevents use of the usual DNSSEC trust anchors. A Device relying on such records MUST use an alternative trust anchor or other means of checking them. Resolvers inside the network should implement RFC 6303 to avoid exposing internal addresses in outside DNS queries.
sections.eli5: A bad guy could give the computer a fake address so it asks the wrong place. The best defense is to double-check the answer another way.

sections.title: IAB Considerations for UNSAF
sections.content:
The IAB requires specifications of UNSAF mechanisms to document a set of considerations. This section applies only to Devices using the method, not to third-party LIS discovery.

  • Exit strategy: when implementations of the RFC 5986 recommendations are widely available, this mechanism can be made obsolete. It is an interim solution for Devices that cannot benefit from them.
  • Brittleness: STUN is inherently brittle with multiple NATs or address realms, and a DNS server that can see the relevant address realm is required. Overlapping address space may give information that is not useful.
  • Experience: existing gateways are reported to give reliable access to STUN and DNS, although DNS response size deserves attention (see RFC 5625).
sections.eli5: This trick is like a temporary bridge. The RFC says up front that it is only meant to be used until a better bridge is built.
